theme: 3 terms on generics: one piece of code for many types

terms.definition: Code that works with many types, so you write it only once.
terms.example: Let's make this function generic, so it works with any type.
terms.code:
func pair<T>(_ a: T, _ b: T) -> [T] { [a, b] }
print(pair(1, 2))

terms.definition: A placeholder name, like `T`, for a type that is chosen when the code is used.
terms.example: I named the type parameter `T`, so the box can hold any type.

terms.definition: A rule that limits a generic to types that follow a protocol.
terms.example: We need a generic constraint here, because the compiler must compare two values.

video.description:
Learn to talk about generics in Swift: Generic, Type Parameter and Generic Constraint, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
Generic - Code that works with many types, so you write it only once.
Type Parameter - A placeholder name, like `T`, for a type that is chosen when the code is used.
Generic Constraint - A rule that limits a generic to types that follow a protocol.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

dialogue.title: One function, any type

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I wrote one function for `Int` and one for `String`, but they look the same.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Make it generic. A generic function works with any type, so you write it once.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: But how does it know the type?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You add a type parameter. Here `T` is the type parameter, a placeholder.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, but `a > b` needs a rule. Add a generic constraint: `T: Comparable`.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Wait, why do we need a generic constraint?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not every type can be compared. Without it, the compiler shows an error.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, I see. The type parameter is `T`, and the generic constraint limits it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Now your generic function works for numbers and text.
Let's make this function generic, so it works with any type.
